title: How to Find Hope When Nothing Changes
excerpt: Some suffering does not end. The prayer goes unanswered for years. Here is how to find a hope that does not depend on the circumstance finally turning.
body:
There is a particular exhaustion that belongs to suffering that does not end. The acute crisis at least has the dignity of drama; people rally, they bring meals, they pray fervently. But the chronic thing, the illness that does not heal, the marriage that does not mend, the prayer prayed for ten years into an apparently empty sky, that suffering wears a different kind of person down. The casseroles stopped long ago. The fervent prayers cooled. And you are left holding a hope that has been disappointed so many times you are afraid to pick it up again. How do you hope when nothing changes? This is the hardest question in this whole subject, and the church's easy answers are useless here.

## Stop pinning your hope on the circumstance

The first thing to understand is that the hope which depends on your situation finally improving is a hope that chronic suffering will eventually break. If your hope is "things will get better," and things do not get better, the hope dies, and you are left with nothing. The Christian hope is built on different ground. Paul wrote some of his most hopeful words from a prison cell he was never released from. His hope was not that the chains would fall off. It was anchored in something the chains could not touch. Move your hope off the circumstance and onto the One who outlasts it.

## Distinguish hope from optimism

Optimism is the belief that things will turn out well, and optimism is a liar in a world like this one. Christian hope is something tougher and stranger. It does not promise that the cancer will go into remission or the prodigal will come home, though sometimes, mercifully, they do. It promises that this is not the end of the story, that the God who raised Jesus from a sealed tomb is at work even where you cannot see it, that the suffering, while real, is not the final word over your life. Hope is not denial of the dark. It is a defiant trust that the dark does not get the last word.

## Grieve the thing that is not changing

Strangely, one of the doors back to hope runs through honest lament. Chronic suffering involves real losses that need to be named and mourned, the life you thought you would have, the version of yourself the suffering took. Let yourself grieve it. "How long, O Lord?" is not a failure of hope. It is the prayer of someone who still believes God is listening, who still expects him to act, who has not yet given up enough to stop asking. Lament and hope are not opposites. Lament is hope refusing to pretend.

## Shrink your horizon and look for the daily mercy

When the big rescue does not come, train your eyes on the small mercies that do. The strength to get through today. The friend who still calls. A moment of unexpected beauty. "His mercies are new every morning," Lamentations says, and notice that this comes from the most sorrowful book in the Bible, a man sitting in the ruins of his city. He is not hoping the ruins will rebuild themselves tomorrow. He is finding, in the rubble, that he is still being carried one more day, and that daily carrying becomes its own kind of hope.

## Anchor in the end of the story

The deepest Christian hope is finally about resurrection, about a day when every wound is healed and every tear is wiped away, and that hope is not escapism. It is the thing that lets a person endure unrelieved suffering without despair, because they know that even if nothing changes in this life, the story does not end in this life. The empty tomb is the guarantee that suffering is temporary and joy is eternal, that the verdict has already been rendered in your favor even while the appeal is still being heard.

**This week:** Each morning, before you let the weight of the unchanged thing settle on you, name one mercy from the day before, one small thing that carried you, however ordinary. Write it down. Build a list across the week. And once this week, read Lamentations 3:19 through 24, where a man in total ruin says "his mercies are new every morning" without any of his circumstances having improved, and let that be the model.

Hoping when nothing changes is the most stubborn form of faith there is. It is not the cheerful certainty that tomorrow will be better. It is the harder, deeper trust that whether or not tomorrow is better, you are held, you are not forgotten, and the story you are in does not end where your suffering does. The morning is coming. It may not be the morning you asked for. It will be a morning, and it will be enough, and the One who promised it has never once broken his word.
